key_factors.text: Spam traffic and a background job overloaded the primary database
Replication broke and the replica fell too far behind to recover
Backups had been failing silently; failure alert emails were rejected
Disk snapshots were not enabled for the database servers
No one owned testing whether backups could actually be restored
An engineer deleted data on the production server instead of the replica

labels.factor: Single-primary database architecture in which a standby is used only for failover, so one database handles all load and acts as a single point of failure; failover replication was also not designed for rapid recovery or protection against accidental data deletion (merged from #13).
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report supports the single-primary/single-point-of-failure setup with a failover-only standby as an underlying architectural weakness, but it is not one of the key factors.

labels.factor: A sustained increase in database load (suspected spam plus a background job removing a flagged account and its data) caused the secondary's replication to lag and fail.
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Describes spam and background-job load overloading the primary and causing the secondary's replication to lag and fail, covering K1 and K2.
key_texts: Spam traffic and a background job overloaded the primary database
Replication broke and the replica fell too far behind to recover

labels.factor: No WAL archiving, so the secondary could not catch up after WAL segments were removed and had to be manually re-synchronised
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Missing WAL archiving meant the replica could not catch up and had to be resynced manually, which is part of the replication breakage in K2.
key_texts: Replication broke and the replica fell too far behind to recover

labels.factor: Insufficient documentation of pg_basebackup behaviour in runbooks and official docs, leading to confusion and misdiagnosis of the hang
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report states the silent-wait behavior of pg_basebackup was undocumented, which caused confusion and led to the second wipe attempt, extending the incident.

labels.factor: Manual, high-risk operations were performed during an incident with no safeguards (such as host-identity checks) to distinguish primary from secondary, so a destructive data directory removal ran on the primary by mistake.
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Describes the destructive directory wipe run on the primary instead of the secondary, matching K6.
key_texts: An engineer deleted data on the production server instead of the replica

labels.factor: Backup procedure silently broken: pg_dump version mismatch with PostgreSQL 9.6 caused every backup to fail without anyone noticing
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Backups failing silently due to pg_dump version mismatch matches the backups-failing-silently factor K3.
key_texts: Backups had been failing silently; failure alert emails were rejected

labels.factor: Failure notifications for backup cronjobs were not delivered because DMARC was not enabled for cronjob emails, so the failure went unnoticed
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Failure notification emails were rejected due to DMARC, directly matching K3's alert-rejection mechanism.
key_texts: Backups had been failing silently; failure alert emails were rejected

labels.factor: Backups were not monitored or regularly verified for existence and restorability, so the lack of any usable backup was discovered only during the incident.
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Lack of verification of backup existence and restorability matches K5 (no ownership of restore testing).
key_texts: No one owned testing whether backups could actually be restored

labels.factor: Disaster recovery relied on snapshots not designed for DR, and Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database servers, leaving only LVM snapshots with a large potential data loss window
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Azure disk snapshots not being enabled for the database servers matches K4.
key_texts: Disk snapshots were not enabled for the database servers

labels.factor: Slow staging storage (throttled network disks) made restoration from snapshot a bottleneck, extending the outage by many hours
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report states slow throttled staging disks made the 18-hour copy the main restoration bottleneck, slowing recovery.

labels.factor: Production configuration left unchanged for a long time (max_connections of 8000) that was unsafe and only surfaced when settings were changed under pressure
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report shows the excessive max_connections setting blocked the PostgreSQL restart during the incident, adding delay to the response.

labels.factor: Single-primary database architecture: one primary handled all production load while the standby served only failover, so load spikes on the primary directly caused replication lag and fragility.
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report describes the single-primary, single-point-of-failure database design handling all load, which is supported as a contributing architectural weakness but is not a distinct answer-key factor.

labels.factor: Sustained, unusually high database load, driven by suspected spam and by a background job that hard-deleted an account flagged for abuse, pushed replication behind. The abuse-handling workflow allowed flagged accounts to be accidentally scheduled for hard deletion, generating heavy background load.
labels.label: match
labels.reason: It describes spam traffic plus a background hard-deletion job overloading the database, matching K1.
key_texts: Spam traffic and a background job overloaded the primary database

labels.factor: No WAL archiving, so once WAL segments were removed from the primary the secondary could only be resynchronised manually, forcing a full re-sync procedure under pressure.
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Replication failed because needed WAL segments were removed and no WAL archiving existed, which matches K2's broken replication that could not recover.
key_texts: Replication broke and the replica fell too far behind to recover

labels.factor: Undocumented, counterintuitive tool behaviour: pg_basebackup silently waits for the primary and creates files in the data directory, and this was not captured in runbooks or official documentation, which led to confusion and a risky troubleshooting path.
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report states pg_basebackup's silent waiting was undocumented, which caused confusion and led to the destructive wipe, though this is not in the key.

labels.factor: Unsafe operational procedures and tooling: nothing in the rebuild process confirmed whether a host was the primary or the secondary before a data directory was wiped, so a destructive command ran on the primary during high-pressure troubleshooting.
labels.label: match
labels.reason: It describes the destructive directory wipe being run on the primary instead of the secondary, matching K6.
key_texts: An engineer deleted data on the production server instead of the replica

labels.factor: Configuration drift and unvalidated settings: max_connections of 8000 had been applied long before and only surfaced as a failure when max_wal_senders was changed and PostgreSQL restarted.
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report supports that max_connections=8000 blocked PostgreSQL restart and delayed the replication fix, though it is not in the key.

labels.factor: Backup process was never verified: the pg_dump backup used a mismatched client version (9.2 vs PostgreSQL 9.6) and failed silently, so no restorable backup existed when needed.
labels.label: match
labels.reason: pg_dump version mismatch caused silent backup failure leaving no restorable backup, matching K3's failing backups and also touching K5's lack of verification.
key_texts: Backups had been failing silently; failure alert emails were rejected

labels.factor: Failure alerting was ineffective: cronjob failure notifications were rejected because DMARC was not enabled, so backup failures went unnoticed for an extended period.
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Cronjob failure emails were rejected due to DMARC so backup failures went unnoticed, directly matching K3's alert emails rejected.
key_texts: Backups had been failing silently; failure alert emails were rejected

labels.factor: Disaster recovery assumptions were not validated: Azure disk snapshots were disabled for database servers on the assumption that other backups were sufficient, and LVM snapshots were not designed for disaster recovery.
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database servers on the assumption other backups sufficed, matching K4.
key_texts: Disk snapshots were not enabled for the database servers

labels.factor: Slow recovery storage: restoration was bottlenecked by cheap, throttled staging disks chosen to save costs, extending recovery time by many hours.
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report states cheap throttled staging disks made the restore take about 18 hours, supporting this as a factor that slowed recovery.

labels.factor: Single primary database with a failover-only secondary meant one database handled all load and was a single point of failure, with no load distribution across hosts
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report states the single primary handling all load was a single point of failure, which is supported context but not an answer-key factor.

labels.factor: Replication lag and failure from unexpected load: WAL segments were removed before the secondary consumed them, and no WAL archiving was in place, requiring manual resynchronisation
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Describes replication lag/failure where WAL segments were removed before the secondary consumed them, matching K2.
key_texts: Replication broke and the replica fell too far behind to recover

labels.factor: The runbooks and official documentation did not describe that pg_basebackup waits silently for the primary to begin streaming, so the expected behaviour was mistaken for a hang
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report says the silent pg_basebackup behavior was undocumented, which led engineers to misdiagnose and take further wiping actions, a supported extra cause.

labels.factor: Manual destructive operations on production had no safeguards (such as host/role verification or confirmation) to distinguish primary from secondary, so a data directory was removed on the primary instead of the secondary

labels.reason: The engineer wiped the data directory on the primary instead of the secondary, matching K6.

labels.factor: Troubleshooting under time pressure involved untested production configuration changes (raising max_wal_senders), which exposed an unreviewed max_connections value of 8000 and caused a restart failure
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report describes the max_connections=8000 setting causing the PostgreSQL restart failure during troubleshooting, which added to the delay.

labels.factor: Backup procedure silently failed because pg_dump version mismatch was not detected, and cron failure notifications were rejected due to DMARC misconfiguration, so failures went unnoticed

labels.reason: Backups silently failed due to pg_dump version mismatch and rejected DMARC failure emails, matching K3.
key_texts: Backups had been failing silently; failure alert emails were rejected

labels.factor: Disaster recovery reliance on snapshots not designed for DR and on slow, cheap storage, which prolonged recovery
labels.label: valid_extra
labels.reason: The report says LVM snapshots weren't meant for DR and slow staging disks caused an 18-hour copy, prolonging recovery.

labels.factor: Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database servers because other backup procedures were assumed to be sufficient, leaving a gap in backup coverage
labels.label: match
labels.reason: Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database servers, matching K4.
